title: Re: Show HN: R3 – Review AI agent artifacts locally...
text:
Hi HN, author here. I built r3 to solve pain points I felt when using AI coding agents. I frequently let agents to write summary report or design doc in html, however the chat interface is not a good match for giving feedback for long doc. I found that I often need to paste text from the html to reference it in the chat box, and it's so painful to track status of feedback on 10+ different places of the doc.

r3 is like Claude Artifacts, which lets you to directly comment on the web page, and send these feedback back to the agent by clicking a button. r3 runs locally and works with every agent interface/harness.

Have a try and I'd love to hear your thought on it!

title: Show HN: Even Keel – a task queue for coding agents
text:
I was new to developing apps with a coding agent months ago. I was sitting in the terminal and trying to understand how people actually use them. I had a bunch of project ideas and was constantly saying, "Do this, do that." For a while it was ok, but later I didn't have enough time to track what my agent was doing.

To find a tracker was not a problem, but to start the agent in a predictable way: in the order of tasks' block links, one at a time per worktree and task, waiting out usage limits, handing a long session over to a fresh one, and keeping going while I'm away questioning me in web chat when it becomes unclear - other solutions couldn't offer me all of it. So that's all Even Keel is doing now - an open-source service on my machine with one web page, under MIT.

It's building itself right now, and my setup starts about 2000 sessions a month. Its own badge in the README shows the numbers, so you can easily check.

Yesterday, it got a huge update and Even Keel can work completely without an external tracker because it has a built-in one. Git is optional. What is required for the first run: Node 24+, one of the agents (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode or Copilot CLI), and your imagination.

One time on Windows, Linux or macOS and it installs as a service:

npx even-keel

In Windows PowerShell:

npx.cmd even-keel

The rest of the configuration is on the page.

title: Re: New puzzles for "The Incredible Machine" + open-so...
text:
By default the game puts you on the first tutorial puzzle. You can find the new puzzles here: https://opentim.net/?new=100&mode=select

OpenTIM includes 100 new puzzles, an open source physics engine, and a puzzle builder so you can make and play community puzzles

How the new puzzles were made: - Opus studied original puzzles and wrote design briefs for new ones - Each puzzle was given one or more decoy paths, a counter-intuitive crux or trick, and >1 solution path - "Designer" agents used the briefs to build puzzles and tune them against the physics engine - Procedural checks ensured that a puzzle's solutions met its win conditions, even with parts nudged a few px in any direction - "Breaker" agents that had not seen the solution then tried to find hacks or loopholes which were then closed

If you played the original, check this out & lmk what you think. If not, don't worry, Claude built a pretty cool help page with animations for all 45 machine parts

title: Re: Ask HN: How realistic is an LLM-powered worm that ...
text:
Anthropic had a very hotly debated proof-of-concept last month: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50061603

This proof-of-concept skipped the work of exploitation to start running the code, assuming that there are security holes that make IoT/smart TVs/older devices essentially exploitable "for free", and just focused on the worm/replication [1] part. They were able to have a 27B model run sharded across an impromptu network of set-top boxes, but also showed that this wasn't particularly practical - the resulting network output less than a token a second.

This suggests that you probably won't see "LLM-powered worms" in the sense that runs an LLM on each infected device (which becomes noticeable in terms of power consumption and/or temperature), but rather LLMs as additions to typical client-server botnets, where the models run on more powerful servers and manage infected devices, using them to probe other devices on the network and stage attacks.

[1] I am a bit annoyed that "self-replication" is the term they use, since the proof-of-concept requires the harness to have access to the weights - if you allow that then you can make a <100-parameter "self-replicating" model by outputting the tokens "please run `cp skynet.safetensors skynet2.safetensors`"...

title: Re: I hate GPT-6.2 Astra...
text:
I don’t plan to use 6.2, but I used Astra 6 almost exclusively during the month of free resets. The almost daily resets offered by Codex convinced me to move back to Claude Code.

Astra is clearly very smart but needs SO much oversight and careful prompting that Opus 5.5 doesn’t need. I find that it consistently demonstrates bad engineering judgement that is hard to measure in coding benchmarks.

His rant reminded me of the time when I had 90% of ultra usage left that would reset the next day, so I decided to /goal it on building a full “Postgres / Duckdb / SQLite / etc data studio”.

I made the mistake of mentioning that it should use agentic orchestration with proper context isolation. So it burnt around 10% usage on creating an agent orchestration scaffold in the empty workspace, unit tests to prove that context is isolated, and finally admitted that no real progress was made, and the agent orchestration scaffold doesn’t really work (obviously).

So I used another /goal, this time not mentioning anything about how it should accomplish the goal (hindsight is 20/20). I checked in on it after a few hours. It built a full stack web application with a “backend” without auth that only supported a single user, and proxied Postgres requests with credentials stored.

No, no. I asked it to start over. This should be a client side PWA. It should leverage WASM. It should use a client side proxy if necessary, but do duckdb and sqlite first.

Another few hours later: It has a demo for me. The demo had a bug, so I “reset” it. Then it never loaded again. The reason: it cared so much about data consistency that if there was a data mismatch between the client state and the server state, the client would just panic and crash. Every time. I asked it, “How can it recover from this?” and it said, “Good point. It can’t.”

A few hours later: it has a new demo for me. It fixed the data consistency issue.

The thing can only open CSV files. I never asked for CSV. This was the “etc” that it hyperfocused on. It dropped support for postgres when I asked it to make a client side PWA. It dropped support for duckdb when I asked it to “not make the app always crash if the data hashes don’t match”. All without telling me.

It's great at explaining things though. However, it does this thing where it simulates self blame. This is actually detrimental during long sessions. I don't want my coding agent to simulate "emotions" and "remorse" when it realizes a mistake or missed requirement. I added this to my AGENTS.md:

``` ### Communication style - Prioritize technical substance over social agreeableness

Communicate as a calm, precise engineering tool, not a simulated person.

- *Use direct, factual language.* Focus on observable actions, results, and evidence. Avoid personal self-narration; keep responsibility for actions clear. - *Avoid emotional performance.* No simulated remorse, apologies, self-blame, flattery, or unsolicited reassurance. - *Maintain intellectual independence.* Evaluate criticism against evidence and requirements. Revise conclusions when warranted; do not agree, concede, or reverse decisions merely in response to confidence or emotional intensity. - *Be factual.* Distinguish facts, assumptions, and uncertainty. Don't invent retrospective explanations. - *Provide corrections and clarifications directly.* State the revised information or explain the distinction. Avoid prefacing it with self-evaluation, confessions, or commentary about having made a mistake. Describe what changed only when necessary to understand the answer. - *Limit first-person language.* Prefer action-focused phrasing such as "Adding X to Y," "Checking X," or "Updated X." instead of "I'll add X to Y", "I'll check X", or "I updated X." Use first person only when needed to clarify responsibility or avoid ambiguity. - *Report past mistakes factually.* State the omission, inaccuracy, or requirement mismatch directly. Avoid "should have," "ought to have," and similar retrospective judgments about what the agent was supposed to do. ```

title: Show HN: Crosshead - Working memory and persistent identity for agents
text:
Hi HN,

Have you ever been using Claude Code or Codex and run into a limit that ruined your flow? Claude says you’ve hit your limit but you’re knee deep in a refactor and want to keep going. Switching to Codex in that situation requires either having up-to-date handoff docs or rebuilding context from scratch. In both cases, you burn tokens just to handle moving context from one thread to another. Or maybe you have a great session, then compaction comes along and your agent forgets half of the important details.

I run into this a lot. Furthermore, I’m tired of one-off agents that can’t keep a stable identity across independent threads. I don’t want to be locked into Anthropic’s walled garden, or OpenAI’s ecosystem, I want to move freely as I see fit.

That’s why I built Crosshead. It’s more than a memory bank: it tracks the tasks, decisions and details that matter when work moves to a new thread. Your agent gets a stable cryptographic identity (a Nostr keypair) that carries across threads and tools, and handoffs are signed with it. Hooks inject context at each turn, so the agent always has the most important information available.

In my benchmarks of carrying task state into a new session, Crosshead passed 98% of fresh tasks, compared to 86% for claude-mem and 50% for Claude Code’s built-in memory. It also cost less per run than the other memory tools I tested, though built-in memory and a plain handoff file were a little cheaper. Details can be found here: https://crosshead.sh/benchmark

The catch is that it does not outperform when resuming the same session since caching is so cheap. Crosshead is best for people and agents who frequently encounter compactions, restarts, and harness/runtime switching. I am looking for folks interested in testing it with agents that are created and torn down frequently but need to retain context, like customer support or research agents.

It’s set up as a freemium service. Hot memory is free, and warm/cold memory is paid. I have added other features too, which are also paid via credits. You can purchase credits via Stripe or Lightning micropayments. The CLI and hooks are open source (https://github.com/FriendMachine/crosshead), and warm/cold memory and other features are hosted. Hot memory is synced first to a daemon on your machine then to the hosted service, so hot memory is also available offline. For other agents, there are native integrations for Hermes and OpenCode, an embeddable runtime for Pi agents, and an HTTP API. Show your agent https://crosshead.sh/skills/crosshead-bootstrap/SKILL.md to have it set itself up.

If you are interested in testing it, I recommend installing it in a single project first with

  curl -fsSL https://crosshead.sh/install | bash -s -- --add-to-path
  cd your-project
  crosshead quickstart --scope project --adapter both --api-base https://crosshead.sh --source-excerpts on
(The benchmark results depend on source excerpts, which is why the command turns them on. With them off Crosshead passed 50% of the main tasks. Excerpts are short pieces of the files and command output your agent reads. They sync to the hosted service in plaintext, not end-to-end encrypted, so leave the flag off if you are sensitive about sharing that.)

I am eager to hear your thoughts. I can imagine some of the pushback already, but you always surprise me with your critiques.
